title: Abijah's Sermon on the Mountain and Victory
summary: Abijah, Rehoboam's son, faces Jeroboam's much larger army and, standing on Mount Zemaraim, preaches to the northern tribes: the LORD gave the kingdom to David's line by a lasting covenant, and Judah has kept the true priesthood and worship that the north abandoned. Caught in an ambush, Judah cries out to the LORD, the priests blow the trumpets, and God routs Israel. Abijah takes Bethel and other towns, and Jeroboam never recovers.
story: Rehoboam's reign ended with ongoing war between north and south (12:15). His son Abijah reigns only three years, and the Chronicler gives his reign a single scene: a battle between the two kingdoms, framed by a speech that states the Chronicler's own convictions about Israel's divided history. The north has the numbers; the south has the covenant with David and the temple worship. Judah wins because it relied on the LORD. The chapter builds on the promises to David in 1 Chronicles 17 and prepares for the longer reign of Abijah's son Asa in chapters 14 to 16.
historical:
Abijah reigned about 913 to 911 BC. The books of Kings call him Abijam and give a brief and negative verdict: he walked in the sins of his father, and his heart was not fully devoted to the LORD (1 Kings 15:1-8). Kings mentions war between Abijam and Jeroboam but tells nothing of this battle or speech. The Chronicler does not contradict the negative verdict so much as leave it unmentioned, choosing to show one moment when Abijah spoke and acted rightly. Readers differ on how to hold the two portraits together: some see the Chronicler drawing on an additional source (he cites a work of the prophet Iddo in verse 22), and others see him presenting Abijah mainly as a mouthpiece for the legitimacy of David's house and the Jerusalem temple.

Mount Zemaraim lay in the hill country of Ephraim, probably near the town of Zemaraim listed in Benjamin's territory (Joshua 18:22), close to the border. Bethel, which Abijah captures, was one of Jeroboam's two royal sanctuaries with a golden calf (1 Kings 12:29). Taking it was a symbolic as well as a military blow, though Bethel later returned to northern control.
cultural:
A covenant of salt (verse 5) was a phrase for a permanent, unbreakable agreement. Salt preserves and does not decay, and it was added to Israel's grain offerings as "the salt of the covenant" (Leviticus 2:13). Numbers 18:19 also uses the phrase for the priests' lasting share of the offerings. Abijah applies it to God's promise to David's house.

Abijah's list of temple duties in verse 11 names the daily routine of Israel's worship as the law described it: burnt offerings each morning and evening, incense on the golden altar, the showbread (twelve loaves set out before the LORD on a gold table each Sabbath, Leviticus 24:5-9), and the lamps of the lampstand lit in the evening. His mockery that anyone who brings a young bull and seven rams can become a priest contrasts Jeroboam's open priesthood with the law's limitation of priesthood to Aaron's descendants. Priests blowing silver trumpets in battle follows Numbers 10:9, which promised that Israel would be remembered before God when the trumpets sounded against an enemy.
literary: The heart of the chapter is Abijah's speech in verses 4 to 12, one of several speeches in Chronicles with no parallel in Kings. It works like a sermon with a legal argument: a claim (the kingdom belongs to David's line), a charge (Jeroboam rebelled and set up false priests and gods), a defense (Judah has kept the LORD's worship), and an appeal (do not fight against the LORD). The phrase "We have not forsaken Him" in verse 10 is answered in verse 11 by "you have forsaken Him", which echoes the forsaking language of chapter 12. The narrative then pays off every claim: the ambush puts Judah in danger, they cry out, the priests blow trumpets, God routs Israel, and verse 18 gives the moral, that Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD.

outline.t: Abijah's reign begins, and two armies face each other
The ambush, the cry to the LORD, and the rout of Israel
Captured cities, Jeroboam's decline, and Abijah's family

doctrines.note: Abijah rests his whole case on God's covenant with David, which he calls a covenant of salt, given to David and his descendants forever. The legitimacy of Judah's king depends on God's promise, not on the size of his army.
Verse 18 says Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD. Faith here is not a feeling but leaning one's weight on God when surrounded, expressed in a cry for help.
The golden calves are called things that are not gods. Worship that God has not appointed, however large its following, cannot save.

words.note: Sha'an, to lean or rely on. The image is of putting one's weight on a support. It appears in verse 18 to explain Judah's victory and will return in chapters 14 and 16, where Asa first relies on the LORD and later relies on the king of Aram instead. The Chronicler uses this verb to test every king.

Melach, salt. In the phrase covenant of salt it stands for permanence and faithfulness. Abijah uses it to claim that God's promise to David's house cannot decay, a claim the Chronicler's readers, living without a Davidic king, would have held on to as hope.

Tsa'aq, to cry out. The word is used for the cry of the oppressed or the desperate, as in Israel's cry in Egypt. When Judah finds itself surrounded, it does not first maneuver; it cries out to the LORD, and the rescue follows.

Chatsotserah, trumpet, the long silver trumpet used by priests (Numbers 10:1-10), not the ram's horn. Priests with trumpets make the battle an act of worship and a summons for God to act, which he does.

christ: Abijah's claim that God gave the kingdom to David and his sons forever is the promise on which the New Testament builds its announcement of Jesus. Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son the throne of his father David and that his kingdom will never end (Luke 1:32-33). The Chronicler's readers had seen David's line lose its throne, yet the book keeps the promise alive, and the gospels present Jesus as the heir in whom it is kept. Abijah's defense of a true priesthood and true worship also points to the letter to the Hebrews, which presents Christ as a high priest appointed by God rather than self-appointed (Hebrews 5:4-6). These connections trace the promise forward; Abijah himself is a flawed king, not a type drawn in detail.

hard.q: Are the numbers in this battle (400,000, 800,000, and 500,000 slain) meant literally?
hard.a: The figures are very large for the population of the region at the time, and readers handle them in several ways. Some take them at face value as accurate counts. Others note that the Hebrew word eleph, usually translated thousand, can also mean a clan or military unit, so the numbers may originally have counted units rather than individual soldiers, which would give much smaller totals. Still others see the numbers as deliberately round and heightened to express the scale of the conflict and of God's deliverance, in keeping with conventions in ancient battle reports. Copyist errors in numbers are also possible, since the Old Testament manuscripts sometimes differ on figures. A related puzzle is Abijah's mother, called Micaiah daughter of Uriel here and Maacah daughter of Abishalom in 1 Kings 15:2; explanations include two names for one woman, or Maacah being a granddaughter of Absalom through Uriel. On any of these views, the point of the chapter stands: a smaller force that relied on God prevailed over a larger one.

questions: Abijah argued that numbers and golden calves could not win against the LORD. What visible strengths are you tempted to trust in over God?
Judah cried out to God only when it was surrounded. What does that suggest about how prayer often begins, and how it might begin earlier?
Kings remembers Abijah as unfaithful, and Chronicles remembers a day he spoke truly. How should we hold together the best and worst of a person's life?
